subjectWorld.label: Subject–world articulation
subjectWorld.definition: The relations by which experience is articulated into identifiable objects, concepts, claims, candidates for knowledge, and commitments about what exists.
subjectWorld.role: It supplies one lexical scope in which appearance becomes object, concept, and proposition; epistemology then assesses the proposition’s standing while ontology states its commitments. The two assessments are independent.
subjectWorld.distinction: It is not a recognized single discipline and not a claim that cognition proceeds through discrete chronological stages. Neural implementation, complete philosophical history, and particular inventories of reality remain outside the boundary.

children.label: Boundary terms
children.definition: The poles and relations presupposed by the bounded context.
children.role: These terms say what is being related before any particular philosophical theory explains the relation.
children.distinction: Their definitions are deliberately neutral between realism, idealism, representationalism, and direct realism.

children.label: Subject
children.definition: The pole to which experience is given and from which intentional acts are lived.
children.role: It locates the first-person ‘from here’ without yet claiming that the subject is a substance, ego, brain, or narrative construction.
children.distinction: Subject means the experiencer as experiencer, not automatically a metaphysical soul or an empirical person.

children.label: World
children.definition: The open, shared horizon within which objects, events, others, and further possible experience belong together.
children.role: World names the encompassing field of intelligibility rather than one more object inside it.
children.distinction: The experienced world is not automatically identical to ‘reality independent of every subject’; that relation is a further philosophical question.

children.label: Reality
children.definition: Whatever is actually the case, whether or not any particular subject believes or experiences it correctly.
children.role: It is the limiting term against which truth and error are understood.
children.distinction: Different metaphysics disagree about whether reality is independent of all experience, partly constituted through it, or inadequately captured by that contrast.

children.label: Articulation
children.definition: Differentiating a field into meaningful units, contrasts, and relations.
children.role: It is the neutral process-word for the whole map: distinguishing, binding, conceptualizing, and asserting.
children.distinction: Articulation need not mean imposing arbitrary divisions on otherwise structureless material; it may disclose, enact, or partly construct structure.

children.label: Map / model
children.definition: An organized representation of selected distinctions and relations in a domain.
children.role: A map compresses a domain by preserving differences relevant to its use.
children.distinction: The cognitive processes build and use maps; an ontology is one kind of map; epistemology evaluates whether beliefs formed through a map deserve acceptance.

children.label: Philosophical lenses
children.definition: Established inquiries that cut across different parts of the subject–world relation.
children.role: There is no single canonical field containing all the nodes below. Transcendental philosophy and phenomenology come closest to unified projects, but each carries specific commitments.
children.distinction: The lenses overlap; the tree assigns each a primary question rather than an exclusive territory.

children.label: Phenomenology
children.definition: The disciplined description of structures of experience as they are lived and given.
children.role: It asks how objects, time, self, others, and world appear, while suspending unsupported claims about what independently causes those appearances.
children.distinction: It is not autobiographical introspection and does not imply that only appearances exist.

children.label: Philosophy of perception
children.definition: The inquiry into what perceptual experience is and how it relates a perceiver to objects, properties, and the world.
children.role: It studies perceptual content, directness, representation, illusion, hallucination, and perception’s epistemic role.
children.distinction: It overlaps phenomenology, philosophy of mind, and epistemology but is not reducible to any one of them.

children.label: Philosophy of mind
children.definition: The inquiry into consciousness, intentionality, mental content, cognition, agency, and their relation to bodies and world.
children.role: It asks what kind of phenomenon perceiving, thinking, remembering, and recognizing are.
children.distinction: It is philosophical analysis; cognitive science supplies empirical accounts of mechanisms.

children.label: Epistemology
children.definition: The inquiry into knowledge, rational belief, evidence, justification, warrant, sources, error, and the limits of inquiry.
children.role: It evaluates the route from experience and concepts to beliefs that claim to be knowledge.
children.distinction: Epistemology is neither the cognitive function that maps patterns to concepts nor a force that warrants a map. It studies what would make particular beliefs warranted.

children.label: Ontology as inquiry
children.definition: The inquiry into the most general kinds and modes of being: what exists, what could exist, and how entities are categorized.
children.role: It examines entities, objects, properties, relations, events, processes, identity, and dependence.
children.distinction: Ontology as inquiry differs from an ontology: a particular proposed inventory and structure.

children.label: Metaphysics
children.definition: The broad inquiry into the most general structure of actuality and possibility.
children.role: It includes ontology and also studies causation, time, modality, persistence, grounding, and dependence.
children.distinction: Ontology is a central part of metaphysics, not usually its whole.

children.label: Transcendental philosophy
children.definition: Inquiry into the conditions that must hold for experience, judgment, knowledge, or objectivity to be possible.
children.role: It asks what the subject–world relation already presupposes rather than explaining it through empirical causal history.
children.distinction: ‘Transcendental’ here means conditions of possibility, not transcendent or supernatural.

children.label: Cognitive science
children.definition: The empirical and computational study of mechanisms enabling perception, learning, categorization, memory, reasoning, and action.
children.role: It can model how articulation is implemented and tested in organisms or machines.
children.distinction: It does not by itself settle phenomenological description, epistemic normativity, or ontology.

children.label: 1. Appearing
children.definition: The field considered only insofar as something is present to experience in some manner.
children.role: This is the descriptive starting point before deciding whether what appears exists independently or is correctly understood.
children.distinction: Appearing is already structured; it should not be imagined as a heap of uninterpreted sensory atoms.

children.label: Experience
children.definition: A lived occurrence for a subject, including perceiving, imagining, remembering, judging, feeling, and acting.
children.role: It is the encompassing genus; perception is one mode of experience.
children.distinction: Having an experience does not by itself make its apparent content true.

children.label: Phenomenon
children.definition: Whatever is considered precisely as it appears or manifests.
children.role: It lets description preserve the appearance without prematurely deciding its mind-independent status.
children.distinction: A phenomenon is not necessarily a private mental image; it may be the worldly object as appearing.

children.label: Phenomenal field
children.definition: The structured totality of what is currently present to experience, including foreground, background, margins, and implicit organization.
children.role: It supplies the region within which attention and perceptual articulation operate.
children.distinction: The field contains more than what is focally noticed or verbally reportable.

children.label: Givenness
children.definition: The manner and degree in which something is present to experience.
children.role: It distinguishes seeing from remembering, imagining, signifying, inferring, or merely anticipating the same object.
children.distinction: Givenness concerns how something appears, not yet whether the appearance is veridical.

children.label: Profile / adumbration
children.definition: The particular aspect through which a spatial object is presently given from one perspective.
children.role: A visible front is one profile of a whole object whose other profiles are not currently seen.
children.distinction: A profile is not a fragment inferred to be a whole; it is the whole object given incompletely through that aspect.

children.label: Horizon
children.definition: The background of absent aspects, contexts, and possible further experiences implicitly belonging to what is given.
children.role: The horizon lets the presently visible profile count as an appearance of a fuller object and world.
children.distinction: The horizon is implicit availability, not a list of explicit predictions.

children.label: Sensation
children.definition: A qualitative sensory occurrence considered apart from recognition of a particular object.
children.role: It can name color, pressure, pitch, or pain before asking what presents or causes it.
children.distinction: Whether perception is built from concept-free sensations is disputed; sensation should not be assumed to be raw, structureless data.

children.label: Attention
children.definition: Selective orientation that foregrounds, sustains, or modulates some content relative to the rest of the field.
children.role: Attention changes resolution and accessibility without necessarily creating its object.
children.distinction: Attention is not identical to consciousness: something may be experienced marginally without focal attention.

children.label: Salience
children.definition: The degree to which something stands out and tends to capture attention.
children.role: Salience explains attraction of attention by contrast, novelty, intensity, or learned significance.
children.distinction: What is salient need not be relevant.

children.label: Relevance
children.definition: The bearing a difference has on a current concern, question, goal, or orientation.
children.role: Relevance selects which contrasts matter for the trajectory of attention.
children.distinction: Something can be relevant without standing out, and salient without being relevant.

children.label: Observation
children.definition: Attention-guided perception undertaken to find out, test, or record something.
children.role: Observation can supply evidence because it is directed by a question and answerable to correction.
children.distinction: An observation is not raw input; its selection and report are already shaped by capacities, concepts, instruments, and aims.

children.label: 2. Perceptual constitution
children.definition: The structures through which appearances are encountered as organized, unified, persisting, meaningful objects.
children.role: This stratum explains how there can be an experienced thing before asking how it is named or justified as knowledge.
children.distinction: ‘Constitution’ means achievement of experiential sense and unity, not fabrication of an external object.

children.label: Perception
children.definition: Experience in which something is presented as presently there.
children.role: Perception gives apparent access to objects and properties and is a primary possible source of knowledge.
children.distinction: This neutral definition does not decide whether perception is direct, representational, conceptual, or nonconceptual.

children.label: Illusion
children.definition: A perceptual case in which a present object or property appears other than it is.
children.role: Illusion separates experiential presentation from veridical perception.
children.distinction: Unlike hallucination, illusion normally involves a corresponding present object that is misperceived.

children.label: Hallucination
children.definition: An experience subjectively as of a present object or event without the corresponding object or event being present.
children.role: It tests whether perceptual character alone guarantees contact with its apparent object.
children.distinction: Hallucination is an epistemic and perceptual category, not by itself a diagnosis or judgment about a person.

children.label: Perceptual organization
children.definition: The differentiation and grouping of the phenomenal field into figures, regions, boundaries, and objects.
children.role: This is the closest standard term for breaking an experiential field into consciously available patterns.
children.distinction: It precedes neither all meaning nor all learning in a simple temporal sense; organization can be immediate and experience-dependent.

children.label: Figure–ground articulation
children.definition: Organization in which one region appears as the focal bounded figure against a supporting background.
children.role: It supplies an inside, an outside, and an asymmetric relation between what is attended and its context.
children.distinction: Figure and ground are relational roles, not permanent properties of regions.

children.label: Grouping
children.definition: Experiencing multiple elements as belonging together because of proximity, similarity, continuity, common movement, or learned structure.
children.role: Grouping creates perceptual units larger than isolated elements.
children.distinction: A perceptual group need not yet be recognized as a named kind.

children.label: Gestalt
children.definition: An organized whole whose experienced structure is not captured by listing independent parts.
children.role: The relations among parts determine the recognizable shape of the whole.
children.distinction: Gestalt does not mean a mystical totality; it names organization with structure-dependent parts.

children.label: Perceptual individuation
children.definition: The experiential separation of one apparent object from another and from its background.
children.role: It establishes countable perceptual units that can later be tracked, recognized, or categorized.
children.distinction: It is not yet the metaphysical criterion of what makes an entity numerically distinct.

children.label: Intentionality
children.definition: The directedness or aboutness through which an experience is of or about something.
children.role: It relates an act of consciousness to an intended object without requiring that the object exist.
children.distinction: Intentionality here does not mean intention in the sense of a plan or purpose.

children.label: Intentional act
children.definition: A concrete episode of perceiving, imagining, remembering, desiring, or judging something.
children.role: It is the act-side of the act–object correlation.
children.distinction: ‘Act’ need not mean a voluntary action; it means a mode of directed experience.

children.label: Noesis
children.definition: The intentional act considered in its particular mode of presenting or meaning something.
children.role: Perceiving, remembering, imagining, and judging can intend the same object with different noetic modes.
children.distinction: Noesis is not merely neural processing or an inner image.

children.label: Intentional object
children.definition: What an intentional act is directed toward, whether real, fictional, absent, possible, or impossible.
children.role: It explains how one can think about Pegasus without committing to Pegasus’s existence.
children.distinction: Intentional existence is being an object of thought, not existing in reality.

children.label: Noema
children.definition: The object precisely as intended or given, together with the sense under which it is intended.
children.role: It distinguishes the tree-as-perceived from the same tree-as-remembered while preserving reference to the same object.
children.distinction: Interpretations of noema are disputed; it should not simply be equated with a mental picture.

children.label: Synthesis
children.definition: The binding of multiple contents, moments, or profiles into one experienced unity.
children.role: Synthesis makes a melody, persisting object, or coherent judgment available as one rather than as disconnected fragments.
children.distinction: It need not be a conscious act of assembling pieces.

children.label: Temporal synthesis
children.definition: The integration of just-past, current, and immediately anticipated phases into a continuous temporal object or event.
children.role: It lets a sequence be heard as one melody and a changing object as continuous.
children.distinction: It is more basic than deliberate recollection or prediction.

children.label: Primal impression
children.definition: The currently occurring phase within temporal experience.
children.role: It is the present edge around which retention and protention are organized.
children.distinction: It is an abstraction within a temporal flow, not an isolated durationless atom.

children.label: Retention
children.definition: The immediate holding-on of the just-elapsed phase as just past.
children.role: Retention keeps the previous note present enough for a melody to be heard.
children.distinction: It is not an act of recalling a completed past event.

children.label: Protention
children.definition: The immediate openness or anticipation toward the next phase of experience.
children.role: Protention gives temporal experience directedness and allows continuation or surprise.
children.distinction: It is not necessarily an explicit forecast.

children.label: Identity synthesis
children.definition: Experiencing different profiles or encounters as presentations of the same object.
children.role: It preserves identity while perspective and appearance change.
children.distinction: It is experiential sameness-across-variation, not yet a metaphysical theory of identity.

children.label: Constitution
children.definition: The structured achievement through which something has stable sense, unity, and validity for consciousness.
children.role: Constitution explains how an object can be experienced as transcending any single appearance.
children.distinction: It does not mean that an isolated mind manufactures the object ex nihilo.

children.label: Object constitution
children.definition: The synthesis through which changing profiles, times, and possible actions belong to one persisting object.
children.role: It produces the experiential identity ‘this same thing’ across incomplete presentations.
children.distinction: Object constitution is prior to naming the thing’s kind, but it may already contain sedimented meaning.

children.label: Sedimentation
children.definition: The settling of previous acts and meanings into habitual, normally unthematic ways of experiencing and understanding.
children.role: Sedimentation lets prior learning silently shape present apperception.
children.distinction: It is retained sense, not necessarily explicit memory.

children.label: Apperception
children.definition: A historical term whose meaning changes: reflective awareness for Leibniz, unified self-consciousness for Kant, and sense-laden apprehension beyond what is directly given for Husserl.
children.role: In the present bounded context, its Husserlian use is closest to experiencing something as more than the currently presented sensory profile.
children.distinction: Apperception is not a stable synonym for categorization; its intended philosopher must be named.

children.label: Leibnizian apperception
children.definition: Reflective or conscious awareness of a perception, contrasted with perceptions too minute or obscure to be noticed.
children.role: It distinguishes merely having a perception from being aware of having it.
children.distinction: Its primary contrast is perception versus consciousness of perception, not pattern versus concept.

children.label: Kantian apperception
children.definition: Self-conscious awareness through which representations can be taken together as mine.
children.role: It grounds the unity required for one subject to judge about one experienced world.
children.distinction: It is not ordinary introspection of a psychological self.

children.label: Transcendental unity of apperception
children.definition: The formal possibility that ‘I think’ can accompany and unify all of a subject’s representations.
children.role: It is a condition for connected experience and objective judgment.
children.distinction: It does not describe a separately perceived inner object called the ego.

children.label: Husserlian apperception
children.definition: Apprehending what is directly presented with a surplus of sense, as an object, type, context, or other subject extending beyond current givenness.
children.role: A visible side is apperceived as the side of a whole thing with unseen sides and familiar possibilities.
children.distinction: It includes interpretation through horizons and sedimented sense but is broader than explicit concept application.

children.label: Appresentation
children.definition: The co-presentation of something not directly given through something that is directly given.
children.role: The unseen back of an object and another person’s subjectivity are available appresentatively.
children.distinction: Appresentation does not make the absent item directly perceived; it presents it through an associated manifestation.

children.label: Representation
children.definition: A state, content, or vehicle that presents, refers to, or stands for something.
children.role: The term can cover concepts, images, propositions, and—in Kant’s broad usage—any mental presentation.
children.distinction: Using the term does not require the inner-picture theory that perception only inspects copies; phenomenological and direct-realist accounts dispute that model.

children.label: 3. Conceptual articulation
children.definition: The stabilization and application of repeatable distinctions that make experience available for classification, inference, and judgment.
children.role: This stratum distinguishes first forming a concept from later recognizing an instance through it.
children.distinction: Conceptual articulation need not create perceptual organization from nothing; perception may already disclose structured wholes.

children.label: Pattern
children.definition: A repeatable organization of differences and relations across one or more cases.
children.role: A pattern can be perceptually detected before it is explicitly conceptualized or named.
children.distinction: A pattern is the recurring structure; a concept is a capacity for discriminating and reasoning with such structure.

children.label: Comparison
children.definition: Relating items under a respect so that similarity, difference, or order becomes available.
children.role: Comparison exposes candidate invariants and contrasts from which concepts may form.
children.distinction: The chosen respect already constrains which differences matter.

children.label: Abstraction
children.definition: Attending to or preserving repeatable features and relations while ignoring other variation.
children.role: Abstraction lets many particulars be handled under one concept.
children.distinction: It is selective compression, not necessarily the invention of a detached entity.

children.label: Concept
children.definition: A repeatable capacity or rule for discriminating, classifying, and drawing inferences about objects, properties, or relations.
children.role: A concept makes a distinction usable across cases and in thought.
children.distinction: A concept is not its word or label; one concept can have several names and a word can express several concepts.

children.label: Intension
children.definition: The content, conditions, or mode of presentation associated with a concept or expression.
children.role: Intension explains what must count for the concept to apply.
children.distinction: It contrasts with extension, the items to which the concept actually applies.

children.label: Extension
children.definition: The set or range of actual items to which a concept or expression applies.
children.role: The extension of ‘tree’ consists of the trees, however the relevant domain is fixed.
children.distinction: Two concepts may have the same extension while differing in intension.

children.label: Concept formation / acquisition
children.definition: The process by which a subject first develops or learns a stable concept.
children.role: Across encounters, a repeatable region of similarity, difference, use, and inference becomes available as one kind.
children.distinction: It is not the later recognition of a new item through an already available concept.

children.label: Category
children.definition: An organized class or kind under which items can be treated as relevantly the same.
children.role: Categories partition or structure a domain for recognition and inference.
children.distinction: ‘Category’ also has stricter meanings in Aristotle and Kant; here it means the general cognitive-logical sense.

children.label: Kind / type
children.definition: A repeatable way of being under which multiple particulars can fall.
children.role: Tree is a kind; this tree is an instance of it.
children.distinction: Whether kinds exist independently of concepts is an ontological question.

children.label: Instance / token
children.definition: A particular occurrence or entity taken as falling under a type or kind.
children.role: It is the this-here case to which a repeatable concept applies.
children.distinction: The same entity may instantiate many kinds under different relevant contrasts.

children.label: Schema
children.definition: An operative pattern that connects a general concept with possible perceptual or practical instances.
children.role: A schema guides what would count as an instance without being a fixed image of one instance.
children.distinction: In Kant, schemata mediate pure concepts and sensible intuition; in cognitive science the term is broader and often means organized prior knowledge.

children.label: Concept application / categorization
children.definition: Taking a present or imagined item as falling under an already available concept.
children.role: This is the mapping from an encountered pattern to a concept: ‘this is a tree.’
children.distinction: It presupposes the concept; it is therefore distinct from concept formation.

children.label: Kind recognition
children.definition: Identifying an item as an instance of a familiar kind.
children.role: It applies a type-level sigil to a present case.
children.distinction: Recognizing this as a tree differs from recognizing it as the same particular tree seen yesterday.

children.label: Reidentification
children.definition: Identifying a currently encountered item as the same particular encountered before.
children.role: It preserves token identity across time, movement, and changing appearance.
children.distinction: It requires more than identifying the item’s kind.

children.label: Misclassification
children.definition: Applying a concept or category to an item for which it is not appropriate.
children.role: It is failure at the pattern-to-concept mapping.
children.distinction: The perceptual object may be correctly individuated even while its kind is misrecognized.

children.label: Conceptualization
children.definition: Making something intelligible under one or more concepts so that it can enter judgment and inference.
children.role: It is the broad process that includes selecting contrasts, applying concepts, and relating them.
children.distinction: Conceptualization is broader than naming and narrower than all perception or sense-making.

children.label: Naming / labeling
children.definition: Associating a linguistic or symbolic sign with an object, concept, category, or position.
children.role: A label makes a distinction addressable and transmissible without reproducing its full interior.
children.distinction: Naming does not by itself form, justify, or guarantee shared possession of the underlying concept.

children.label: Judgment
children.definition: The act of committing to something as being the case.
children.role: Judgment turns conceptual articulation into a truth-assessable claim.
children.distinction: Merely entertaining or imagining a content is not yet judging it true.

children.label: Proposition
children.definition: The truth-assessable content expressed by a declarative claim and capable of being believed, denied, or inferred.
children.role: Different sentences or mental acts can express the same proposition.
children.distinction: A proposition is not identical to its sentence or to the psychological event of judging it.

children.label: Inference
children.definition: A transition from one or more accepted contents to another content because the former are taken to support the latter.
children.role: Inference extends articulation beyond what is directly perceived or remembered.
children.distinction: Logical validity concerns support between contents; epistemic warrant also depends on the standing of the premises and method.

children.label: Conceptual scheme
children.definition: An interconnected system of concepts and inferential relations through which a domain is articulated.
children.role: It makes some distinctions, descriptions, and questions available while backgrounding others.
children.distinction: A conceptual scheme is a structure of intelligibility, not automatically the structure of what exists.

children.label: Sense-making
children.definition: The activity of rendering a situation intelligible enough for orientation, expectation, communication, or action.
children.role: It coordinates perception, concepts, context, affect, and practical relevance.
children.distinction: It is broader and less technically precise than categorization, apperception, or epistemology.

children.label: 4. Epistemic evaluation
children.definition: Assessment of whether claims and beliefs deserve acceptance, how strongly, from which sources, and with what vulnerability to error.
children.role: This stratum concerns the standing of claims made through a map, not the cognitive act of drawing the map.
children.distinction: Truth, confidence, justification, reliability, warrant, and knowledge are different contrasts and must not be collapsed.

children.label: Epistemic process
children.definition: A process that forms, preserves, or updates beliefs and can contribute to knowledge.
children.role: Perception, memory, testimony, introspection, and inference are candidate epistemic processes.
children.distinction: A process can be cognitive without being knowledge-producing, and its study is not itself epistemology.

children.label: Sources of belief or knowledge
children.definition: Routes by which a subject acquires or preserves epistemically assessable contents.
children.role: Core candidates are perception, memory, testimony, introspection, and inference.
children.distinction: Calling something a source does not guarantee that every output from it is knowledge.

children.label: Perception as source
children.definition: Perceptual experience used as prima facie support for beliefs about present objects and events.
children.role: It links appearance to empirical belief.
children.distinction: Its support can be defeated by evidence of illusion, poor conditions, or unreliable processing.

children.label: Memory
children.definition: The capacity to preserve or recover contents from earlier experience or learning.
children.role: Memory normally transmits prior epistemic standing rather than creating truth by itself.
children.distinction: Remembering differs from Husserlian retention, which holds the immediately elapsed phase of present experience.

children.label: Testimony
children.definition: Acquiring belief from what another subject communicates as being the case.
children.role: It distributes knowledge across subjects and institutions.
children.distinction: Its warrant depends on speaker, channel, context, and social norms, not only on the listener’s private evidence.

children.label: Introspection
children.definition: Attention directed toward one’s own current or recent mental states.
children.role: It can support beliefs about what one seems, thinks, feels, or intends.
children.distinction: Introspection is not infallible and is not identical to phenomenology as a philosophical method.

children.label: Inference as source
children.definition: Deriving a belief from other beliefs or evidence through deductive, inductive, abductive, or probabilistic support.
children.role: It yields conclusions not directly presented by perception or memory.
children.distinction: Inference can transmit error when its premises or transition are defective.

children.label: Belief
children.definition: A stance that takes a proposition to be true.
children.role: Beliefs are primary bearers of justification and candidates for knowledge.
children.distinction: Belief is not the same as confidence, truth, acceptance for practical purposes, or knowledge.

children.label: Claim
children.definition: A proposition asserted or otherwise put forward as true.
children.role: Claims make beliefs publicly answerable to reasons, evidence, disagreement, and correction.
children.distinction: A proposition can be entertained without being claimed.

children.label: Truth
children.definition: The correctness of a proposition with respect to how things are.
children.role: Knowledge is normally factive: what is known must be true.
children.distinction: Truth is not the same as evidence, consensus, certainty, or justification; theories disagree about its deeper nature.

children.label: Evidence
children.definition: Information or experience that changes the rational support for a proposition.
children.role: Evidence can confirm, disconfirm, discriminate among, or leave claims underdetermined.
children.distinction: Evidence is always evidence relative to a claim and background assumptions; it is not simply any available data.

children.label: Justification
children.definition: The positive epistemic standing a belief has when it is responsibly supported by adequate reasons, evidence, or method.
children.role: It answers why holding this belief is epistemically permissible or rational for the subject.
children.distinction: A belief can be justified yet false, and true yet unjustified.

children.label: Warrant
children.definition: A theory-dependent name for the positive epistemic property or process that makes a true belief knowledge rather than merely lucky truth.
children.role: It marks the missing success condition beyond truth and belief; some philosophers use it more loosely as justification or entitlement.
children.distinction: Epistemology studies warrant; epistemology does not itself confer warrant on a map.

children.label: Reliability
children.definition: The tendency of a belief-forming process to produce true rather than false beliefs across relevant cases.
children.role: Reliability can explain epistemic standing even when the subject cannot state all reasons for trusting the process.
children.distinction: Reliable processes can err in particular cases, and defining the relevant range of cases is itself difficult.

children.label: Knowledge
children.definition: Epistemically successful cognition of what is the case; at minimum, knowledge is normally taken to exclude falsity and accidental correctness.
children.role: Knowledge is the target status whose conditions epistemology tries to understand.
children.distinction: There is no universally accepted complete analysis of knowledge.

children.label: Factivity
children.definition: The principle that if a subject knows a proposition, that proposition is true.
children.role: Factivity distinguishes knowledge from sincere but false belief.
children.distinction: Factivity does not imply certainty or infallibility in judging whether one knows.

children.label: Justified true belief
children.definition: The proposal that knowing requires believing a true proposition with justification.
children.role: It isolates three central conditions: belief, truth, and epistemic support.
children.distinction: Gettier cases show that these conditions can coincide through luck and therefore may not be sufficient.

children.label: Gettier problem
children.definition: The problem that a belief can be justified and true while being true only through epistemic luck.
children.role: It motivates accounts of warrant, reliability, safety, proper function, and anti-luck conditions.
children.distinction: It challenges the sufficiency, not the usual necessity, of justified true belief.

children.label: Epistemic luck
children.definition: Accidental alignment between a belief and truth that is insufficiently connected to the way the belief was formed.
children.role: Removing the wrong kind of luck is a central constraint on knowledge.
children.distinction: Not every contingency is disqualifying; the problem is truth that the method did not properly secure.

children.label: Basis of cognition
children.definition: The distinction between cognition grounded in experience and cognition whose warrant does not depend on particular experiences.
children.role: It separates a posteriori from a priori warrant.
children.distinction: The distinction concerns epistemic basis, not merely when a belief was first learned.

children.label: A posteriori
children.definition: Known or justified through dependence on empirical experience.
children.role: Ordinary perceptual knowledge is paradigmatically a posteriori.
children.distinction: A posteriori does not mean uncertain or subjective.

children.label: A priori
children.definition: Known or justified independently of any particular empirical experience, though experience may be needed to acquire the concepts involved.
children.role: Logical and mathematical claims are common candidates.
children.distinction: A priori does not simply mean innate or temporally prior.

children.label: Defeater
children.definition: Information that removes or reduces the justification or warrant of a belief.
children.role: Learning that the lighting distorts color can defeat a color judgment that was initially reasonable.
children.distinction: A defeater can undermine the source or support an incompatible claim.

children.label: Underdetermination
children.definition: A condition in which the available evidence is compatible with multiple incompatible claims or theories.
children.role: It prevents evidence alone from selecting one map without further assumptions, inquiry, or practical constraints.
children.distinction: Underdetermination need not make every option equally plausible.

children.label: Skepticism
children.definition: A challenge to whether knowledge or adequate justification is possible in some domain.
children.role: Skeptical scenarios test what connects appearance, belief, and world strongly enough for knowledge.
children.distinction: Methodological doubt is a tool; global skepticism is the stronger claim that knowledge is unavailable.

children.label: Objectivity
children.definition: Validity not exhausted by one subject’s present perspective and answerable to shared constraints across perspectives or inquiry.
children.role: Objectivity connects first-person givenness to claims intended to hold beyond the current viewpoint.
children.distinction: Objectivity need not mean a view from nowhere or the absence of all subjects.

children.label: Intersubjectivity
children.definition: The structure in which multiple subjects can encounter, communicate about, and correct one another concerning a shared world.
children.role: It supplies a route by which private appearances participate in public objectivity.
children.distinction: Agreement alone does not guarantee truth; intersubjectivity provides shared accessibility and correction.

children.label: Confidence / certainty
children.definition: Confidence is degree of belief; certainty is maximal or defeat-resistant confidence or epistemic security, depending on theory.
children.role: These terms describe strength or security of commitment.
children.distinction: High confidence can accompany falsehood, and knowledge need not require psychological certainty.

children.label: 5. Ontological articulation
children.definition: The inventory, categories, and dependence relations implied when a conceptual scheme or theory is taken as describing what there is.
children.role: This stratum states the map’s commitments rather than how the subject acquired or justified them.
children.distinction: An ontology can be explicit and formal or tacit in ordinary practice; its correctness remains an epistemic and metaphysical question.

children.label: An ontology
children.definition: A proposed inventory of entities, categories, relations, and constraints for a domain or for reality generally.
children.role: It says what kinds of things the map treats as available and how they can relate.
children.distinction: An ontology is the account or model; ontology as inquiry studies and compares such accounts.

children.label: Ontic / ontological
children.definition: Ontic concerns particular beings and facts about them; ontological concerns their modes, categories, or conditions of being.
children.role: ‘The tree is damaged’ is ontic; ‘what makes something an object persisting through change?’ is ontological.
children.distinction: The distinction is especially important in Heidegger, where ontology also asks about the meaning of Being.

children.label: Entity
children.definition: Anything an ontology counts as being in some sense.
children.role: Entity is the maximally general placeholder before a more specific category is assigned.
children.distinction: Not every ontology treats every entity as a substance-like object.

children.label: Particular
children.definition: An individual, nonrepeatable entity or occurrence: this tree, this event, this sound.
children.role: Particulars are candidates for numerical identity and instantiation of repeatable kinds or properties.
children.distinction: A particular can change properties while remaining numerically the same, if the ontology permits persistence.

children.label: Universal
children.definition: A repeatable property, relation, or kind that can be instantiated by multiple particulars.
children.role: Universals explain how distinct particulars can literally share a feature or type.
children.distinction: Realists accept universals in some form; nominalists deny that repeatable words require repeatable entities.

children.label: Object
children.definition: An entity treated as a unified bearer of identity, properties, relations, and possible change.
children.role: Objects are central units for reference, predication, tracking, and action.
children.distinction: Events, processes, relations, fields, and institutions may be entities without fitting every theory’s model of an object.

children.label: Property
children.definition: A way an entity is, such as being green, massive, fragile, or triangular.
children.role: Properties support predication, similarity, difference, and change.
children.distinction: Theories disagree whether properties are universals, tropes, sets, dispositions, or conceptual constructions.

children.label: Relation
children.definition: A way two or more entities stand with respect to one another, such as larger-than, beside, causes, or represents.
children.role: Relations articulate structure that cannot be assigned to isolated entities alone.
children.distinction: Whether relations exist independently of their relata or conceptualization is theory-dependent.

children.label: Kind as ontological category
children.definition: A repeatable mode or grouping that an ontology treats as belonging to the structure of its domain.
children.role: It turns a cognitive category into a claim about how entities themselves are organized.
children.distinction: A category can be useful for cognition without corresponding to a mind-independent natural kind.

children.label: Natural kind
children.definition: A grouping taken to reflect objective structure that supports explanation, induction, or lawful regularity.
children.role: Natural kinds are candidates for being discovered rather than merely stipulated.
children.distinction: Which groupings qualify, and how independent they are of inquiry, remain disputed.

children.label: Constructed kind
children.definition: A grouping whose existence or boundaries substantially depend on human practices, purposes, institutions, or classifications.
children.role: It explains real patterns that would not have the same structure without those practices.
children.distinction: Constructed does not mean imaginary, arbitrary, or causally ineffective.

children.label: Event
children.definition: An occurrence or change located in time, often with participants and conditions.
children.role: Events provide units for causation, explanation, and temporal ordering.
children.distinction: An event is often bounded; a process emphasizes temporally extended unfolding.

children.label: Process
children.definition: An organized, temporally extended becoming or activity.
children.role: Process ontologies treat change and activity as basic rather than as secondary modifications of stable substances.
children.distinction: A process can have phases and continuity without being a persisting object in the ordinary sense.

children.label: State of affairs / fact
children.definition: A structured way entities, properties, or relations obtain: the tree’s being beside the house.
children.role: A fact is normally a state of affairs that obtains and can make a proposition true.
children.distinction: Theories disagree whether facts are entities in addition to the things and relations composing them.

children.label: Identity
children.definition: The relation in which something is numerically the same entity as itself, including questions of sameness across change and description.
children.role: Identity permits reidentification, counting, reference, and persistence claims.
children.distinction: Qualitative similarity is sharing features; numerical identity is being one and the same entity.

children.label: Ontological individuation
children.definition: The criteria that make an entity this individual rather than another.
children.role: It answers what fixes the unit and its boundary in the ontology.
children.distinction: Perceptual individuation separates apparent units; ontological individuation states what actually makes one entity distinct.

children.label: Persistence
children.definition: The conditions under which an entity remains the same through time and change.
children.role: Persistence explains how properties can change while reference to one entity continues.
children.distinction: Different theories model persistence through enduring wholes, temporal parts, processes, or continuity relations.

children.label: Modality
children.definition: The structure of actuality, possibility, impossibility, contingency, and necessity.
children.role: Modality distinguishes what is the case from what could, must, or cannot be the case.
children.distinction: Modal claims add more than descriptions of what happens to be actual.

children.label: Actuality
children.definition: What is in fact the case.
children.role: Actuality supplies the realized region against which alternatives are considered.
children.distinction: Actual does not mean necessary; much of what is actual could have been otherwise.

children.label: Possibility
children.definition: What could be the case under the relevant modal constraints.
children.role: Possibility structures alternatives, affordances, counterfactuals, and explanation.
children.distinction: Logical, physical, practical, and epistemic possibility use different constraints.

children.label: Necessity
children.definition: What must be the case and could not be otherwise under the relevant modal constraints.
children.role: Necessity marks invariant structure across the relevant possible alternatives.
children.distinction: Logical necessity differs from physical, metaphysical, and practical necessity.

children.label: Ontological commitment
children.definition: The entities and categories a claim, theory, or practice must treat as existing for its assertions to be true or intelligible.
children.role: It exposes what a map presupposes: objects, events, numbers, meanings, institutions, or other entities.
children.distinction: Using a word does not automatically commit one to a corresponding entity; commitment depends on the theory’s inferential and quantificational structure.

children.label: Realism
children.definition: The view, in some domain, that its entities or truths do not depend for their existence or truth on our recognition, beliefs, or conceptual decisions.
children.role: Realism treats at least some structure as discovered and capable of resisting our maps.
children.distinction: Realism can be local to a domain and does not imply naive access or perfect knowledge.

children.label: Idealism
children.definition: A family of views assigning mind, experience, or conditions of intelligibility a constitutive role in what can count as an object or world.
children.role: Idealism challenges the picture of a fully articulated world whose structure is wholly independent of any possible experience.
children.distinction: It does not simply mean that everything is imaginary; Kantian and Husserlian idealisms preserve constraints and objectivity.

children.label: Conceptualism
children.definition: The view that universals, kinds, or generality depend in some way on conceptual capacities rather than existing as wholly independent abstract entities.
children.role: It places category structure at the subject–world interface.
children.distinction: Conceptualism need not deny the existence of particulars or the world’s resistance to arbitrary classification.

children.label: Social construction
children.definition: Dependence of an entity, category, boundary, or fact on collective practices, norms, language, institutions, or recognition.
children.role: It explains how shared articulation can become part of the real causal and normative world.
children.distinction: Socially constructed does not mean individually invented, unreal, or easily changed.

children.label: Reification
children.definition: Treating an abstraction, relation, process, or useful distinction as though it were a self-standing thing with stronger existence than the account warrants.
children.role: It is a characteristic failure in moving from conceptual usefulness to ontological commitment.
children.distinction: Not every abstraction is a false entity; reification is the unearned conversion of a conceptual role into a thing.

children.label: Category mistake
children.definition: Treating something as belonging to a logical or ontological category for which the applied question or predicate makes no sense.
children.role: It reveals that a map’s types have been crossed rather than that an ordinary factual answer is merely false.
children.distinction: Asking where the university is after seeing all its colleges is the classic shape: the organization is mistaken for one more building.

mind.label: Mind
mind.core: The organized family of capacities and states through which a subject or system may experience, select, represent, remember, learn, value, coordinate, and act.
mind.contrast: Mind is not one faculty. Consciousness, sentience, attention, cognition, intelligence, agency, and selfhood can vary independently.
domains: Philosophy of mind
The bearer or organization of mental states, capacities, contents, and causal powers.
Phenomenology
The lived field and structures through which subject, object, self, others, and world appear.
Cognitive science
An architecture of information-bearing processes enabling perception, memory, learning, reasoning, and control.
Neuroscience
Capacities and states realized by biological mechanisms; the term itself does not name one anatomical system.
AI
A functional attribution to an artificial system. Intelligence or agency does not by itself establish consciousness or sentience.

children.label: Basic structural vocabulary
children.core: The minimal terms needed to say how an experiential or cognitive field becomes intelligible.
children.contrast: Articulation is the operation; an object is a resulting unity; a concept is a reusable way of distinguishing or understanding such unities.

children.label: Articulation
children.core: The differentiation and organization of a field into identifiable units, contrasts, boundaries, and relations.
children.contrast: Articulation is not merely naming. A distinction can be perceptually or practically operative before a word is attached, and the differentiation need not be arbitrary.
domains: Phenomenology
The field comes to presence as figure and ground, object and horizon, same and different, before or beneath explicit judgment.
Cognitive science
Includes segmentation, grouping, individuation, categorization, and relational organization.
Philosophy of language
Also means making an already available distinction explicit and communicable in signs or propositions.
Attention Language
Relevant contrasts constrain a region until it is available to attention as one recognizable, pointable sigil.

children.label: Object
children.core: A unified something that can be attended to, tracked, referred to, acted upon, or made the subject of predication.
children.contrast: Object does not mean only physical thing. An event, number, fictional character, remembered scene, or possibility can be an object of thought; an intentional object need not exist in reality.
domains: Phenomenology
The pole of identity synthesized across changing profiles and acts: the same tree as seen, remembered, or imagined.
Ontology
An entity treated as bearing identity, properties, relations, and possible change; not every ontology makes every entity an object.
Cognitive science
An individuated, task-relevant unity represented or tracked across variation.
AI
Object detection or representation is a functional grouping under a task ontology, not proof that the system has discovered the final joints of reality.

children.label: Entity
children.core: Anything an ontology counts as being or existing in some sense—the maximally general placeholder for what the ontology quantifies over or posits.
children.contrast: Entity is broader than object and is not the same as essence. Depending on the ontology, properties, relations, events, processes, numbers, or institutions may be entities without being object-like things.
domains: Ontology
The neutral highest-level term used before assigning a more specific category such as object, event, property, relation, or process.
Phenomenology
An intentional object can be meant without being a real entity; thinking about Pegasus does not add Pegasus to the ontology.
Data modeling
‘Entity’ often means a modeled identity-bearing record or domain unit, a much narrower technical use.
Russian
In philosophical Russian, entity is usually «сущее»; «сущность» normally translates essence. In data modeling, however, entity is conventionally «сущность».

children.label: Concept
children.core: A reusable capacity or rule for distinguishing, classifying, and drawing inferences about a kind, property, relation, or structure.
children.contrast: A concept is neither the articulation process nor the object articulated. It is the repeatable form through which this and later objects can be understood in the same respect.
domains: Cognitive science
A learned structure supporting categorization, prediction, generalization, and inference.
Logic
A condition or content determining what falls under it and which inferences its application licenses.
Language
A word may express a concept, but words and concepts are not identical.
Attention Language
A concept is closest to a reusable type-shaped sigil; applying it recognizes a present region through that stabilized shape.

children.label: Levels of description
children.core: Distinct ways of describing the same candidate mental event or capacity: how it feels, what the person does, what function is performed, and how it is implemented.
children.contrast: A correlation or behavioral test at one level is not automatically an explanation or identity claim at another.
domains: Use
Name the level before comparing theories or transferring a term between humans, animals, brains, and machines.

children.label: Phenomenological level
children.core: Description of how an experience is lived and given from the subject’s perspective.
children.contrast: It describes experiential structure, not its neural cause or behavioral measurement.
domains: Phenomenology
Includes phenomenal character, intentionality, temporal flow, embodiment, horizon, self-givenness, and world-givenness.

children.label: Conditions of possibility
children.core: Structures or capacities without which a specified kind of experience, judgment, knowledge, or objectivity could not occur as such.
children.contrast: A condition of possibility need not be an earlier event that causes the phenomenon. It can be a constitutive relation presupposed by the phenomenon’s very intelligibility.
domains: Example
Temporal synthesis is not an event occurring before a melody; it is part of what makes successive sounds experienceable as one melody.
Method
First specify the phenomenon, then ask what must already hold for that phenomenon to be possible in the relevant sense.

children.label: Transcendental
children.core: Concerning the enabling conditions under which experience, knowledge, objects, or objectivity are possible for a subject.
children.contrast: Transcendental does not mean beyond experience or supernatural. It turns back from an intelligible phenomenon to the structures that make it possible.
domains: Kant
Inquiry into a priori forms and functions—such as space, time, categories, and unity of apperception—that make experience and objective judgment possible.
Husserl
Inquiry into intentional, temporal, embodied, and intersubjective constitution through which objects and world acquire sense and validity for consciousness.
Compression
Transcendental asks: what must the subject–world relation already contain for this appearance or claim to have its present form?

children.label: Transcendent
children.core: Going beyond a specified boundary, domain, or possible mode of access.
children.contrast: Unlike transcendental, transcendent points beyond the field; it does not analyze the field’s enabling structure.
domains: Kant
What lies beyond the bounds of possible experience, when treated as an object of supposed knowledge.
Theology / metaphysics
What exceeds the finite, empirical, worldly, or immanent order.
Phenomenology
A perceived object is sometimes called transcendent because it exceeds every profile currently given, even though it appears within experience.

children.label: Immanent
children.core: Remaining within or belonging to the relevant field, process, experience, or order.
children.contrast: Immanent is the direct contrast to transcendent, not to transcendental.
domains: Phenomenology
What is given within the stream or structure of experience, though philosophers differ about exactly what counts as immanent.
Compression
Transcendent crosses the boundary; immanent remains within it; transcendental asks what makes the boundary and its contents possible.

children.label: Personal level
children.core: Explanation of a whole subject through perceptions, beliefs, desires, reasons, intentions, emotions, and actions.
children.contrast: It attributes intelligible states to the person or agent, not to an isolated neuron or module.
domains: Philosophy
Associated with reason-giving and rational or practical explanation.

children.label: Subpersonal level
children.core: Explanation through processes or components below the level of the whole subject.
children.contrast: Subpersonal mechanisms process information but need not themselves believe, see, decide, or experience in the personal sense.
domains: Cognitive science
Examples include feature extraction, predictive updating, memory consolidation, and control loops.

children.label: Functional level
children.core: Description by the role a state or process plays among inputs, other states, and outputs.
children.contrast: Functional equivalence does not by itself settle whether implementations share phenomenal character.
domains: AI
Most claims about model attention, memory, planning, and agency are functional claims.

children.label: Computational level
children.core: Description in terms of represented variables, transformations, algorithms, objectives, and information flow.
children.contrast: Computation is one possible form of functional realization, not a synonym for cognition or consciousness.
domains: AI
Specifies what an artificial system calculates and how internal states are transformed.

children.label: Neural / biological level
children.core: Description through cells, circuits, dynamics, bodies, physiology, and their causal organization.
children.contrast: Finding a neural correlate does not yet explain why or how the correlated experience occurs.
domains: Neuroscience
Connects mental capacities to biological realization and causal intervention.

children.label: Behavioral level
children.core: Description through observable actions, reports, performance, learning curves, and responses to perturbation.
children.contrast: Behavior supplies evidence about mind but is not simply identical to experience or cognition.
domains: AI
Benchmarks operationalize capacities behaviorally; passing one does not fix the mechanism or phenomenal status.

children.label: Normative / social level
children.core: Description through reasons, obligations, responsibility, recognition, institutions, and socially assigned status.
children.contrast: Normative standing is not reducible to raw performance, though performance and capacities may matter to it.
domains: Ethics
Sentience, agency, autonomy, and personhood support different kinds of moral consideration.

children.label: Operationalization
children.core: A specified observable procedure or measurement used as evidence for an otherwise abstract construct.
children.contrast: The operational measure is an indicator of the construct, not necessarily its complete meaning.
domains: Example
A report or discrimination task may operationalize awareness without defining consciousness as reportability.

children.label: Correlate
children.core: A variable or process that systematically covaries with another.
children.contrast: Correlation alone does not establish cause, mechanism, identity, or sufficiency.
domains: Neuroscience
A neural correlate of consciousness is a minimal neural condition systematically associated with a conscious content or level.

children.label: Mechanism
children.core: An organized set of entities and activities that causally produces or sustains a phenomenon.
children.contrast: A mechanism explains more than a predictor or correlate because its organized operation makes a difference to the outcome.
domains: Cross-domain
Mechanistic explanation connects subpersonal or neural organization to functional and behavioral capacities.

children.label: Realization / implementation
children.core: The concrete organization in which a functional capacity or state is instantiated.
children.contrast: One abstract function may admit multiple realizations; whether phenomenality is multiply realizable remains disputed.
domains: AI
Software, model weights, runtime state, hardware, sensors, and environment jointly realize system capacities.

children.label: Experience & consciousness
children.core: Terms concerning whether and how anything is lived or present for a subject.
children.contrast: Experience must be separated from wakefulness, attention, reportability, intelligence, and behavioral responsiveness.

children.label: Consciousness
children.core: An umbrella term for subjective experience, availability of mental content, or the overall condition of a conscious subject; the intended sense must be named.
children.contrast: Consciousness is not automatically wakefulness, attention, self-consciousness, intelligence, language, or report.
domains: Analytic philosophy
Commonly divided into phenomenal consciousness and access consciousness, and into creature and state consciousness.
Phenomenology
The lived field in which intentional objects, self, time, body, others, and world are given.
Cognitive science
Often operationalized through report, flexible access, integration, discrimination, and control.
Neuroscience
Studied through level, content, neural correlates, causal mechanisms, and dissociations among arousal, report, and awareness.
AI
A contested attribution. Functional fluency, attention mechanisms, self-report, or intelligence alone do not establish phenomenality.

children.label: Phenomenal consciousness
children.core: The presence of subjective qualitative experience—there being something it is like for the subject.
children.contrast: It concerns experienced character, not merely information being available for reasoning or report.
domains: Phenomenology
Roughly overlaps lived givenness, though phenomenology usually analyzes richer intentional structure rather than isolating bare qualia.
AI
This is the disputed property at issue when asking whether a machine actually experiences rather than merely processes.

children.label: Phenomenal character
children.core: The particular way an experience feels or appears from the first-person perspective.
children.contrast: It is the structure or character of an experience, not the external object or the subject’s report about it.
domains: Example
The look of a red surface, the painfulness of pain, or the spatial openness of a room.

children.label: Qualia
children.core: A contested term for individual qualitative features of experience, such as a particular redness or painfulness.
children.contrast: Some theories treat qualia as intrinsic mental atoms; others reject that picture while retaining phenomenal character.
domains: Phenomenology
Often regarded as too atomistic if it detaches qualities from intentional object, body, horizon, and world.

children.label: Subjectivity
children.core: The first-personal mode in which experience is given to or lived by a subject.
children.contrast: Subjectivity does not mean arbitrariness, unreliability, or isolation from a shared world.
domains: Ethics
A subject of experience is a candidate bearer of welfare because things can matter experientially to it.

children.label: Access consciousness
children.core: A mental content’s availability for reasoning, deliberate control, flexible action, and usually report.
children.contrast: Access can be operationally tested; whether it always coincides with phenomenal experience is disputed.
domains: Cognitive science
Often modeled through global availability, working memory, decision, and report systems.
AI
Systems can display functional access without that settling whether anything is experienced.

children.label: Creature consciousness
children.core: The condition of an organism or system being conscious at a time.
children.contrast: It concerns the subject’s global condition, not whether one particular representation is conscious.
domains: Neuroscience
Compared across wakefulness, sleep, anesthesia, coma, and related states.

children.label: State consciousness
children.core: The property of a particular perception, thought, feeling, or representation being conscious.
children.contrast: A conscious creature can contain many nonconscious mental processes and states.
domains: Cognitive science
Research asks which contents enter experience or access while others remain subliminal or unattended.

children.label: Self-consciousness
children.core: Awareness of oneself as oneself, ranging from implicit first-personal givenness to explicit reflection on one’s traits or current state.
children.contrast: It is a further organization of consciousness, not a prerequisite for every conscious experience.
domains: Phenomenology
Distinguishes pre-reflective self-awareness from making oneself an explicit object of reflection.
Psychology
Can mean self-recognition, self-monitoring, autobiographical self-knowledge, or concern with how one appears to others.
AI
Self-description, self-modeling, and metacognitive monitoring are functional capacities, not conclusive evidence of phenomenal selfhood.

children.label: Pre-reflective self-awareness
children.core: The implicit first-personal givenness of experience as mine while attention is directed toward its object.
children.contrast: It is not observing or representing oneself as a separate object.
domains: Example
While absorbed in music, the listening is tacitly lived from here without an explicit thought about oneself.

children.label: Reflective self-consciousness
children.core: The explicit act of taking oneself, one’s state, or one’s activity as an object of attention and judgment.
children.contrast: Reflection thematizes what was previously lived implicitly.
domains: Example
Noticing that I am anxious, distracted, or listening.

children.label: Metaconsciousness / meta-awareness
children.core: Explicit awareness of the current contents or quality of one’s own conscious experience.
children.contrast: One can be conscious of an object without currently noticing what one’s own experience is doing.
domains: Cognitive science
Used in studies of mind wandering, meditation, confidence, and error monitoring.

children.label: Sentience
children.core: The capacity for subjective experience, especially affectively valenced experience such as pain, pleasure, comfort, or distress.
children.contrast: Sentience does not require high intelligence, language, explicit self-awareness, rational agency, or personhood.
domains: Ethics / animal welfare
Commonly the capacity for suffering or enjoyment and therefore a basis for welfare interests and moral consideration.
Philosophy of mind
Sometimes used broadly for any phenomenal consciousness; authors should state whether neutral sensory experience counts.
Biology
Inferred from converging behavioral, physiological, neural, and evolutionary evidence rather than one response alone.
AI
Should name possible capacity for experience, not mere responsiveness, language ability, or autonomous behavior.

children.label: Awareness
children.core: A loose term for registration, availability, responsiveness, or conscious experience of something.
children.contrast: Without a qualifier, awareness fails to distinguish phenomenal experience from functional access or behavioral sensitivity.
domains: Phenomenology
Usually means lived awareness of an object, field, or one’s own experience.
Cognitive science
May mean information available to report or control, sometimes operationally defined without metaphysical commitment.
Neuroscience
Often paired with arousal as the content dimension of consciousness, but usage is not uniform.
AI / engineering
‘Context-aware’ commonly means functionally sensitive to variables, not conscious of them.

children.label: Arousal / wakefulness
children.core: The organism’s global physiological activation and capacity to sustain waking responsiveness.
children.contrast: Arousal is not the same as conscious content or awareness: the dimensions can dissociate.
domains: Clinical neuroscience
Used in assessing sleep, anesthesia, coma, unresponsive wakefulness, and minimally conscious states.
Affective science
Affective arousal instead means intensity or activation of an emotional state; the two uses must be separated.

children.label: Level of consciousness
children.core: The global degree or condition in which conscious experience and responsiveness are possible.
children.contrast: It is distinct from which particular content is conscious.
domains: Neuroscience
Common contrasts include wakefulness, sleep stages, anesthesia, coma, unresponsive wakefulness, and minimally conscious states.

children.label: Content of consciousness
children.core: What is presently experienced: a color, sound, thought, pain, object, mood, or scene.
children.contrast: Content varies within a level and need not include explicit awareness of the experiencing self.
domains: Research
Content-specific paradigms compare neural or functional states when one stimulus rather than another is experienced.

children.label: Nonconscious / unconscious processing
children.core: Information-sensitive processing that affects cognition or behavior without the relevant content being consciously experienced or accessed.
children.contrast: Nonconscious does not mean nonexistent, inactive, irrational, or psychoanalytic repression.
domains: Cognitive science
Includes priming, automatic motor adjustment, perceptual processing, and implicit learning.
Psychoanalysis
‘The unconscious’ names a much richer dynamic system of wishes, conflict, defense, and symbolic formation.
AI
Most internal computation is not ‘unconscious’ in a phenomenal sense unless consciousness has independently been established.

children.label: Selection & attention
children.core: Terms concerning which signals, objects, actions, or goals receive priority within finite processing and control.
children.contrast: Selection can alter consciousness but is not identical to consciousness.

children.label: Attention
children.core: Selective prioritization of some information, object, location, task, or action for enhanced processing or control.
children.contrast: Attention is neither consciousness nor simple looking: attention can be covert or nonconscious, and experience can exceed focal attention.
domains: Phenomenology
A modulation of the experiential field that foregrounds, sustains, or shifts what is thematic.
Cognitive science
A family of selection, amplification, suppression, orienting, and resource-allocation processes.
Neuroscience
Implemented by distributed interacting systems rather than one attention center.
AI
An attention mechanism computes weighted routing or aggregation among representations; it does not imply awareness or caring.

children.label: Selective attention
children.core: Prioritizing target information while competing information is reduced, delayed, or excluded.
children.contrast: It describes competition and selection, not necessarily a single limited resource.
domains: Example
Following one voice in a noisy room or one feature in a visual display.

children.label: Sustained attention / vigilance
children.core: Maintaining readiness and task-relevant selection over time.
children.contrast: It is temporal stability of attention, not simply high arousal.
domains: Example
Monitoring a display for rare changes.

children.label: Divided attention
children.core: Coordinating attention across more than one task or source.
children.contrast: It rarely means equal full-capacity processing; performance depends on interference, automatization, and task structure.
domains: Cognitive science
Used to study dual-task costs and capacity limits.

children.label: Endogenous / top-down attention
children.core: Selection guided by current goals, expectations, instructions, or voluntary orientation.
children.contrast: It contrasts with capture driven primarily by stimulus properties.
domains: Attention Language
Closest to relevance-led orientation toward a currently inhabited goal or sigil.

children.label: Exogenous / bottom-up attention
children.core: Rapid selection captured by salient or unexpected stimulation.
children.contrast: It need not align with the subject’s current goal or relevance structure.
domains: Example
A flash or sudden sound pulls orientation.

children.label: Executive attention
children.core: Control of attention where goals, habits, responses, or representations conflict.
children.contrast: It is one component of cognitive control, not the whole of executive function.
domains: Example
Maintaining the task rule while suppressing a dominant but wrong response.

children.label: Overt / covert attention
children.core: Overt attention moves sensory organs or body toward a target; covert attention shifts priority without the corresponding visible movement.
children.contrast: Where the eyes point and what is attended often correlate but are not identical.
domains: Example
Monitoring something in peripheral vision while gaze remains fixed.

children.label: Machine-learning attention
children.core: A differentiable mechanism that assigns context-dependent weights when combining or routing representations.
children.contrast: The technical name is an analogy to selective weighting; it does not establish phenomenal attention, awareness, or agency.
domains: Transformers
Queries, keys, and values compute weighted mixtures that make some represented relations more influential for the next computation.

children.label: Salience
children.core: The property by which a signal stands out and tends to capture or recruit processing.
children.contrast: Salience is not relevance: what captures attention may not matter to the current concern.
domains: Perception
May arise from contrast, novelty, intensity, motion, or learned significance.
Neuroscience
Salience-network language concerns detecting and coordinating behaviorally significant events; it should not be reduced to visual conspicuity.

children.label: Relevance
children.core: The relation by which a difference matters to a current concern, question, goal, or trajectory.
children.contrast: Relevance is goal-relative and can guide attention even when the relevant signal is not salient.
domains: Attention Language
Relevance supplies the vector that selects affordances and constrains which contrasts become active.
Cognitive science
Related to task set, value, expected information gain, and goal-dependent priority.

children.label: Orienting
children.core: Redirecting sensory receptors, attention, or bodily readiness toward a location, object, or event.
children.contrast: Orienting is a shift toward a target; sustained attention is maintaining selection after the shift.
domains: Phenomenology
Changes the center and horizon of the experienced field.

children.label: Cognitive control
children.core: Goal-dependent regulation of attention, memory, response selection, and task rules.
children.contrast: Control is a functional capacity and need not be consciously supervised at every step.
domains: Relation
Executive attention resolves competition; cognitive control includes broader maintenance, switching, monitoring, and inhibition.

children.label: Aboutness & mental content
children.core: Terms concerning how a mental state is directed toward, presents, or says something about an object, situation, or possibility.
children.contrast: Aboutness must be distinguished from phenomenal feel, causal input, and goal-directed intention.

children.label: Intentionality
children.core: The directedness or aboutness through which a mental state is of, about, or toward something.
children.contrast: Intentionality does not mean intention as a plan, and its object need not exist.
domains: Phenomenology
