The act–object correlation: every experience has a mode of intending and something as intended.
Analytic philosophy
The problem of how mental or linguistic states acquire content and reference.
AI
Internal states can carry functional or interpreted content without this alone establishing consciousness.

children.label: Intentional object
children.core: What a mental act is directed toward, whether present, absent, fictional, possible, or impossible.
children.contrast: Being intended does not imply existing in reality.
domains: Example
One can fear a possible event or imagine Pegasus.

children.label: Noesis
children.core: The act-side of intentional experience considered in its mode: perceiving, remembering, imagining, judging, desiring.
children.contrast: Noesis is not a neural representation or a voluntary action.
domains: Relation
Noesis correlates with noema, the object as intended in that mode.

children.label: Noema
children.core: The object as intended or given, together with the sense under which it is intended.
children.contrast: It should not simply be treated as an inner picture; interpretations of its exact status differ.
domains: Relation
The same tree can be intended perceptually, imaginatively, or memorially with different noematic sense.

children.label: Mental content
children.core: What a mental state represents, means, or is about.
children.contrast: Content is not identical to the physical vehicle or event that carries it.
domains: Semantics
May be conceptual or nonconceptual, propositional or imagistic, narrow or environmentally dependent.
AI
Can mean information encoded or functionally used by a system; whether that is intrinsic or observer-relative is disputed.

children.label: Mental representation
children.core: A state or structure that carries content and can stand in for an object, property, situation, or possibility within cognition.
children.contrast: Representation does not require a picture-like inner copy, and some enactive approaches reject representation as the basic model.
domains: Cognitive science
Posited to explain perception, memory, concepts, prediction, and planning.
AI
Vectors, tokens, maps, latent states, and symbolic structures can function representationally within a task architecture.

children.label: Perception
children.core: Experience or processing that presents and tracks objects, properties, and events as currently available in the environment or body.
children.contrast: Perception is not merely sensation, belief, or passive reception; theories dispute how conceptual and action-dependent it is.
domains: Phenomenology
World-presenting intentional experience with perspective, horizon, and embodied possibilities.
Cognitive science
Inference- and action-sensitive extraction of useful structure from sensory signals.
AI / robotics
Transformation of sensor data into task-usable estimates or representations; no phenomenal implication follows automatically.

children.label: Sensation
children.core: A qualitative sensory occurrence or modality-specific response considered apart from full object recognition.
children.contrast: Sensation is not necessarily raw, structureless, or consciously experienced.
domains: Phenomenology
Qualities are ordinarily given within an organized field and object, not as isolated atoms.
Neuroscience
Sensory transduction and processing can occur without reportable sensation.

children.label: Imagination
children.core: The capacity to present, explore, or transform possibilities without taking them as presently perceived or necessarily actual.
children.contrast: Imagination is not limited to visual imagery and does not require belief in what is imagined.
domains: Phenomenology
An intentional mode with different givenness from perception and memory.
Cognition
Supports simulation, counterfactual reasoning, planning, creativity, and perspective-taking.
AI
Generation of novel internal candidates is functionally analogous; phenomenal imagery should not be inferred from output generation.

children.label: Thought
children.core: A mental episode or state in which content is entertained, combined, judged, questioned, or manipulated.
children.contrast: Thought can be conscious or nonconscious, linguistic or nonlinguistic, propositional or imagistic.
domains: Phenomenology
Inner speech is one possible phenomenal vehicle of thought, not thought’s universal form.

children.label: Concept
children.core: A repeatable capacity or rule for discriminating, categorizing, and reasoning about a kind, property, or relation.
children.contrast: A concept is not its word, image, prototype, or extension, though any may help realize or express it.
domains: AI
A decodable feature or cluster may correlate with a concept; stable inferential use is a stronger criterion than mere linear separability.

children.label: Propositional attitude
children.core: A subject’s stance toward a truth-assessable content: believing, desiring, hoping, fearing, or intending that something be the case.
children.contrast: The same proposition can be held under different attitudes.

children.label: Belief
children.core: A stance that takes a proposition to be true and disposes cognition or action accordingly.
children.contrast: Belief is not identical to knowledge, certainty, verbal assertion, or a momentary thought.
domains: AI
Calling an internal state a belief is usually functional or interpretive unless a richer agent-level architecture is specified.

children.label: Desire
children.core: A state that represents or treats some outcome as to-be-brought-about, obtained, preserved, or avoided.
children.contrast: Desire concerns direction of fit toward changing the world; belief aims to fit how the world is.
domains: AI
Objectives and reward functions can play desire-like functional roles without implying felt wanting.

children.label: Cognition & competence
children.core: Terms concerning information-sensitive transformation, reasoning, problem solving, adaptation, and task competence.
children.contrast: Cognition can be nonconscious; intelligence can exist without sentience; performance does not identify mechanism.

children.label: Cognition
children.core: The family of processes enabling perception, categorization, memory, learning, reasoning, decision, language, and control.
children.contrast: Cognition is broader than conscious thought and does not imply phenomenal experience.
domains: Philosophy
Can mean concept- and reason-involving mental activity, sometimes contrasted with affect or perception.
Cognitive science
Includes conscious and nonconscious information-processing capacities.
AI
Used functionally for task-relevant transformation and control; whether machine cognition is literal or analogical depends on theory.

children.label: Intelligence
children.core: Capacity to learn, generalize, reason, adapt, and achieve goals across a relevant range of environments or tasks.
children.contrast: Intelligence is competence, not consciousness, sentience, wisdom, autonomy, or moral worth.
domains: Psychometrics
A latent capacity inferred from structured covariance among cognitive-task performances.
Cognitive science
A profile of learning, abstraction, control, transfer, and problem-solving capacities.
AI
Operationalized through performance and generalization relative to tasks, resources, and environments; benchmark breadth is not unrestricted generality.

children.label: Understanding
children.core: A grasp of how elements and relations fit together that supports explanation, inference, counterfactual variation, and transfer.
children.contrast: Understanding is stronger than storing an answer or matching a surface pattern, but no single accepted operational test fixes it.
domains: Epistemology
Often treated as grasping explanatory or dependency structure, possibly distinct from propositional knowledge.
AI
Disputed between behavioral-functional accounts and accounts requiring grounding, agency, embodiment, or consciousness.

children.label: Reasoning
children.core: The organized use of representations or commitments to derive, compare, revise, or justify conclusions.
children.contrast: Reasoning need not be formally valid, verbally explicit, or conscious throughout.
domains: Logic
Evaluated by relations of support such as validity or probabilistic coherence.
Psychology
A process subject to heuristics, biases, working-memory limits, and learned strategies.
AI
Can be implemented symbolically, probabilistically, neurally, through search, or through hybrid architectures.

children.label: Inference
children.core: A transition from accepted information to a conclusion because the former is taken to support the latter.
children.contrast: Inference is the transition relation; reasoning is the broader activity in which inferences are generated and assessed.
domains: Kinds
Deduction preserves truth under validity; induction generalizes; abduction selects an explanatory hypothesis.

children.label: Problem solving
children.core: Transforming an initial state into a goal state under constraints when the route is not immediately available.
children.contrast: Problem solving is task-relative competence, not a general measure of consciousness or understanding.
domains: AI
May use search, decomposition, planning, learned policies, tools, or external representations.

children.label: Planning
children.core: Constructing or selecting an ordered, conditional, or hierarchical organization of actions toward a goal.
children.contrast: A plan is a representation or policy for possible action, not the action itself or a guarantee of execution.
domains: AI
Ranges from explicit symbolic search to implicit policy structure and model-predictive control.

children.label: Decision-making
children.core: Selecting among actions, hypotheses, or commitments under goals, values, uncertainty, and constraints.
children.contrast: Decision is the selection outcome or commitment; choice often emphasizes the available alternatives and agentive act.
domains: AI
Decision rules optimize or satisfice relative to an objective, model, policy, or learned value structure.

children.label: Executive function
children.core: The family of capacities for maintaining goals, inhibiting responses, switching tasks, updating working memory, and monitoring performance.
children.contrast: It is a family of control functions, not a single inner executive or homunculus.
domains: Relation
Executive attention handles attentional conflict; executive function includes broader regulation across cognition and action.

children.label: Metacognition
children.core: Monitoring and regulating one’s own cognition, confidence, strategies, errors, and limits.
children.contrast: Metacognition can be functionally present without full explicit self-consciousness and can itself be inaccurate.
domains: Psychology
Includes confidence judgments, error monitoring, strategy selection, and judgments of learning.
AI
Self-evaluation, uncertainty estimation, critique, and control loops are metacognitive functions; they do not establish sentience.

children.label: Creativity
children.core: Capacity to produce ideas, interpretations, or artifacts that are both novel relative to a context and fitting to relevant constraints.
children.contrast: Novelty alone is randomness; usefulness or aptness alone is routine competence.
domains: AI
Generative novelty can be measured behaviorally; authorship, intention, and experiential imagination are separate questions.

children.label: Cognitive flexibility
children.core: Capacity to change rules, representations, strategies, or perspectives when context or goals change.
children.contrast: Flexibility differs from instability: the shift is responsive to relevant constraints.
domains: Relation
Supports transfer, reframing, task switching, and recovery from a failed model.

children.label: Memory & learning
children.core: Terms concerning preservation, reconstruction, acquisition, and change of capacities across time.
children.contrast: Memory is not a literal archive, and learning is not restricted to conscious instruction.

children.label: Memory
children.core: The family of capacities by which prior experience or learning alters present availability, expectation, skill, recognition, and action.
children.contrast: Memory is reconstructive and distributed; it is not one store containing faithful copies of the past.
domains: Phenomenology
Remembering is a present intentional act that gives something as past; it differs from retention of the just-elapsed present.
Cognitive science
Divided by duration, content, access, and function into interacting systems.
AI
Can mean context state, retrieval stores, learned parameters, recurrent state, or external records; these are different mechanisms.

children.label: Working memory
children.core: Limited-capacity active maintenance and manipulation of information for an ongoing task.
children.contrast: It is not identical to all short-term storage or to consciousness, though access often overlaps.
domains: AI
A context window is an engineering analogy to accessible task state, not a complete model of human working memory.

children.label: Episodic memory
children.core: Memory for personally experienced events situated in a particular temporal-spatial context.
children.contrast: It differs from knowing a fact without re-presenting an experienced episode.
domains: Phenomenology
Often includes a sense of pastness and a first-person perspective on the remembered event.

children.label: Semantic memory
children.core: Memory for facts, meanings, concepts, and general knowledge not tied to one remembered learning episode.
children.contrast: It is distinct from episodic recollection even when episodic experience originally produced the knowledge.
domains: Example
Knowing that Rome is in Italy without recalling when one learned it.

children.label: Procedural memory
children.core: Retention of skills, habits, and action dispositions expressed in performance.
children.contrast: One may know how without being able to state the procedure propositionally.
domains: Example
Typing, balancing, or playing an instrument.

children.label: Autobiographical memory
children.core: The integrated memory system through which events and self-knowledge are organized as one’s life history.
children.contrast: It combines episodic and semantic material and is shaped by present identity and narrative.
domains: Self
Supports continuity of the narrative and personal self without alone constituting numerical identity.

children.label: Explicit / implicit memory
children.core: Explicit memory is intentionally retrievable and reportable; implicit memory is expressed through performance without deliberate recollection.
children.contrast: Implicit does not mean weak, unconscious in every respect, or inaccessible to all measurement.
domains: Examples
Recall of a fact is explicit; priming and many skills are implicit.

children.label: Learning
children.core: Relatively durable change in knowledge, representation, expectation, policy, or capacity due to experience, practice, or feedback.
children.contrast: Learning is change in competence or organization, not merely temporary performance change or storing one observation.
domains: Biology / psychology
Includes associative, perceptual, motor, conceptual, social, and explicit learning.
AI
Parameter, policy, representation, or memory change driven by data and an update rule; subjective experience is not implied.

children.label: Conditioning
children.core: Learning predictable relations among stimuli, responses, and consequences.
children.contrast: Conditioning is not necessarily passive or mindless, and it does not exhaust learning.
domains: Kinds
Classical conditioning concerns predictive stimulus relations; operant conditioning concerns consequences of action.

children.label: Reinforcement learning
children.core: Learning action policies or value estimates from temporally distributed consequences.
children.contrast: A numerical reward signal is a training variable, not necessarily pleasure, desire, or moral reward.
domains: Biology
A family of learning models related to prediction error, value, and action selection.
AI
An agent updates policy or value to improve expected cumulative reward under an environment model or interaction history.

children.label: Statistical learning
children.core: Extraction of regularities, distributions, sequences, or latent structure from exposure.
children.contrast: Regularity learning need not be consciously noticed or verbally expressible.
domains: Relation
Supports perceptual grouping, language acquisition, prediction, and representation learning.

children.label: Recall
children.core: Producing or reconstructing remembered content with limited direct cueing.
children.contrast: Recall differs from recognition, where a presented candidate is judged familiar or previously encountered.
domains: Example
Answering an open question versus selecting the answer from options.

children.label: Recognition memory
children.core: Identifying a presented item or event as previously encountered.
children.contrast: Recognition of prior occurrence differs from recognizing an item’s category or meaning.
domains: Components
Can involve familiarity, recollection, or both.

children.label: Forgetting
children.core: Loss, inaccessibility, transformation, or failure of previously available memory.
children.contrast: Failure to retrieve at one moment does not prove that every memory trace or influence is absent.
domains: Functions
Forgetting can reduce interference and update relevance, not only represent breakdown.

children.label: Affect & valuation
children.core: Terms concerning how states and possibilities matter positively or negatively to a subject or control system.
children.contrast: Valuation, reward, felt pleasure, motivation, emotion, and suffering must remain distinct.

children.label: Affect
children.core: The broad domain of valenced and activating states through which situations feel good, bad, urgent, calm, attractive, or aversive.
children.contrast: Affect is broader than named emotion and is not the opposite of cognition.
domains: Affective science
Often organized by valence and arousal, with emotion and mood as more structured forms.
Phenomenology
Affective orientation discloses what matters and changes the field of affordances and relevance.
AI
Affective labels or value signals can play functional roles without implying felt affect.

children.label: Valence
children.core: The positive–negative dimension of experience, evaluation, or motivational significance.
children.contrast: Valence is not intensity: a mildly pleasant and intensely pleasant state share direction but differ in magnitude.
domains: Sentience
Capacity for valenced experience is the narrower welfare-relevant sense of sentience.

children.label: Affective arousal
children.core: The activation or intensity dimension of an affective state, from subdued to highly activated.
children.contrast: It is not identical to neurological wakefulness, although the two can interact.
domains: Example
Calm pleasure and excited pleasure can share positive valence while differing in arousal.

children.label: Feeling
children.core: The consciously lived aspect of an affective, bodily, or evaluative state.
children.contrast: A system can compute value or prepare action without necessarily feeling that valuation.
domains: Relation
An emotion may include feeling, appraisal, physiology, expression, and action tendency; feeling is its experienced aspect.

children.label: Emotion
children.core: A coordinated episode involving appraisal, bodily change, action tendency, expression, attention, and often conscious feeling toward something significant.
children.contrast: Emotion is not merely a private feeling or a fixed reflex; theories weight its components differently.
domains: Phenomenology
A world-directed way in which situations and affordances show up as threatening, joyful, shameful, desirable, and so on.
Neuroscience
Implemented by distributed systems supporting appraisal, bodily regulation, learning, salience, and action.
AI
Emotion models can coordinate priorities and behavior functionally without resolving phenomenal feeling.

children.label: Mood
children.core: A comparatively diffuse and enduring affective orientation that colors the field without requiring one focal object.
children.contrast: Mood differs from a brief object-directed emotion, though the two influence one another.
domains: Phenomenology
A mood changes which affordances, expectations, and meanings are available across the world as a whole.

children.label: Appraisal
children.core: Evaluation of an event or situation relative to concerns, goals, norms, coping possibilities, and agency.
children.contrast: Appraisal can be rapid and nonconscious; it need not be a verbal judgment.
domains: Role
Helps explain why the same event produces different emotions for different subjects or contexts.

children.label: Interoception
children.core: Sensing and regulating the internal condition of the body.
children.contrast: Interoception is broader than consciously feeling organs and includes nonconscious regulation.
domains: Relation
Contributes to affect, hunger, thirst, pain, arousal, bodily selfhood, and sense of presence.

children.label: Pain
children.core: An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential bodily damage, or resembling such experience.
children.contrast: Pain is not identical to nociception, tissue damage, withdrawal behavior, or a verbal report.
domains: Phenomenology
A valenced bodily experience that can reorganize attention, agency, space, time, and world.
Ethics
Pain is a central but not exhaustive form of welfare-relevant suffering.
AI
Damage signals or avoidance policies are not sufficient evidence of felt pain.

children.label: Nociception
children.core: Detection and processing of noxious or potentially tissue-damaging stimulation.
children.contrast: Nociception can occur without conscious pain, and pain can occur without current nociceptive input.
domains: Sentience
Reflexive nociception alone is weaker evidence of sentience than converging evidence of flexible, integrated aversive experience.

children.label: Pleasure
children.core: Positively valenced experience that is liked, enjoyed, or experienced as good.
children.contrast: Pleasure is not identical to reward prediction, wanting, preference, or reinforcement.
domains: Affective neuroscience
Liking, wanting, and learning are distinguishable processes even when they normally interact.

children.label: Suffering
children.core: Sustained or significant negatively valenced experience that burdens, threatens, or frustrates the subject.
children.contrast: Suffering is broader than nociceptive pain and can involve fear, grief, helplessness, deprivation, or conflict.
domains: Ethics
Its possibility depends on sentience; its forms may also depend on memory, anticipation, selfhood, and social meaning.

children.label: Reward
children.core: A consequence or signal that increases, evaluates, or guides action selection and learning within a system.
children.contrast: Reward is a functional role or variable, not automatically pleasure, approval, desire, or moral value.
domains: Neuroscience
Reward processing includes prediction, learning, motivation, and hedonic components that can dissociate.
AI
A scalar or structured objective signal used to update policy or evaluate outcomes.

children.label: Motivation
children.core: Processes that energize, prioritize, sustain, or redirect behavior toward and away from outcomes.
children.contrast: Motivation is not identical to conscious desire, pleasure, intention, or action.
domains: AI
Objective functions and policies can create motivation-like functional organization without felt wanting.

children.label: Drive
children.core: A regulatory pressure associated with bodily or learned needs that biases attention and action.
children.contrast: Drive is one source of motivation and need not be consciously represented as a goal.
domains: Examples
Hunger, thirst, thermoregulation, and some learned compulsions.

children.label: Agency & action
children.core: Terms concerning goal-directed control, commitment, choice, skill, and attribution of action to an agent.
children.contrast: Agency is not equivalent to consciousness, intelligence, autonomy, responsibility, or mere causal activity.

children.label: Agent
children.core: A system treated as maintaining orientations or goals and selecting actions in relation to an environment.
children.contrast: Being usefully modeled as an agent does not by itself establish consciousness, sentience, selfhood, autonomy, or moral responsibility.
domains: Philosophy
Often implies action attributable to reasons, intentions, or control capacities.
Biology
Organisms exhibit adaptive self-maintaining action without every behavior requiring deliberation.
AI
A functional architecture that observes, updates state, selects actions, and affects an environment under objectives and constraints.

children.label: Agency
children.core: The capacity for behavior or events to count as attributable, goal-directed action of a subject or system.
children.contrast: Agency differs from mere causal movement; stronger notions add reasons, reflective control, autonomy, or responsibility.
domains: Phenomenology
Includes the lived sense of initiating and controlling action within an affordance field.
Cognitive science
Coordinated perception–action control under goals, models, and feedback.
AI
Usually functional goal-directed interaction; the strength of attribution depends on persistence, control, adaptation, and independence.

children.label: Action
children.core: An event attributable to an agent as something it does, rather than merely something that happens to it.
children.contrast: Not every bodily movement or system output is an action in the full reason-responsive sense.
domains: Analysis
Theories distinguish intentional action, skilled action, habitual action, and basic versus mediated action.

children.label: Goal
children.core: A represented, embodied, or externally specified state toward which action and evaluation are organized.
children.contrast: A goal need not be consciously entertained, and an objective assigned by a designer need not be the system’s own endorsed goal.
domains: Psychology
Goals organize attention, planning, persistence, monitoring, and emotion.
AI
May be encoded as reward, loss, target condition, instruction, policy constraint, or evaluator.

children.label: Intention
children.core: A commitment or plan that organizes present or future action toward an outcome.
children.contrast: Intention is not intentionality: intention concerns action commitment; intentionality is the aboutness of any mental state.
domains: Phenomenology
Can be lived as directed readiness or practical orientation, not only as a verbal plan.
AI
An intention-like state is a persistent action commitment within an agent architecture, not evidence of conscious resolve.

children.label: Volition
children.core: The initiation, endorsement, or control of action as willed by the subject.
children.contrast: Volition is narrower than motivation and does not require unconstrained metaphysical freedom.
domains: Phenomenology
Often concerns the felt transition from possibility or intention into enacted movement.

children.label: Choice
children.core: Selection among represented or practically available alternatives attributable to an agent.
children.contrast: Choice requires an alternative structure; it need not be fully conscious, rational, or free from constraint.
domains: Decision theory
Models choice as preference- and belief-sensitive selection under uncertainty and resource limits.

children.label: Control
children.core: Capacity to regulate a process or action so that deviations are detected and corrected relative to a reference or goal.
children.contrast: Control can be distributed and automatic; it does not require an inner controller or conscious supervision.
domains: AI / robotics
Feedback, models, policies, and constraints jointly determine effective control.

children.label: Autonomy
children.core: Capacity to govern action through relatively self-maintained goals, reasons, or norms rather than immediate external command.
children.contrast: Autonomy comes in degrees and is not equivalent to unsupervised operation, unpredictability, or independence from all environment.
domains: Ethics
Often requires reflective endorsement, competence, and freedom from controlling interference.
Robotics / AI
Usually means operational independence over a task range; this is weaker than moral autonomy.

children.label: Affordance
children.core: An action possibility available to an agent in virtue of relations among its capacities, environment, and current situation.
children.contrast: An affordance is neither merely an objective feature nor merely a subjective idea; it is relational.
domains: Phenomenology
Affordances are experienced as invitations, resistances, paths, tools, or threats within a meaningful world.
Attention Language
Relevance selects which affordances advertise entry into the next sigil.

children.label: Skill
children.core: A learned, reliable, context-sensitive capacity for effective action.
children.contrast: Skill is not merely explicit rule knowledge; expertise often reduces the need for focal deliberation.
domains: Phenomenology
Skilled coping can be directly responsive to affordances without representing every step as a proposition.

children.label: Habit
children.core: A sedimented disposition to perceive, feel, or act in familiar ways under recurring conditions.
children.contrast: Habit is not necessarily rigid automation; it can be flexible and world-sensitive.
domains: Phenomenology
Habitual capacities shape what immediately appears possible and familiar.

children.label: Sense of agency
children.core: The experience that I am initiating, controlling, or authoring an action or thought.
children.contrast: The feeling of agency can diverge from actual causal control and from retrospective attribution of responsibility.
domains: Research
Studied through prediction, action–outcome matching, perturbation, and explicit judgments of control.

children.label: Free will
children.core: A disputed capacity for control over action sufficient for some form of genuine choice or moral responsibility.
children.contrast: It is not settled simply by showing neural causation, unconscious preparation, randomness, or subjective effort.
domains: Positions
Compatibilists locate freedom within reason-responsive causal control; incompatibilists require stronger alternatives or sourcehood.

children.label: Self & continuity
children.core: Terms concerning the pole, ownership, embodiment, model, narrative, and persistence to which experiences and actions are attributed.
children.contrast: Subject, self, ego, personality, personal identity, and personhood answer different questions.

children.label: Subject
children.core: The first-personal pole to which experience is given and from which intentional life is lived.
children.contrast: The subject need not be conceived as a separately observable substance, narrative, personality, or body-object.
domains: Phenomenology
The subject is primarily the ‘from here’ of appearing, not one more item appearing inside the field.

children.label: Self
children.core: The organized unity to which experiences, body, memories, traits, commitments, and actions are attributed as mine.
children.contrast: There may be multiple layers of selfhood; no single self-object need underlie all of them.
domains: Phenomenology
Minimal first-personal and embodied structures of experience.
Psychology
Self-concept, autobiographical organization, traits, goals, and social identity.
Neuroscience
Distributed processes supporting body ownership, agency, autobiographical memory, perspective, and self-relevance.
AI
Self-models and persistent identity structures can be functional without establishing a phenomenal subject.

children.label: Minimal self
children.core: The immediate first-personal unity, ownership, and agency implicit in current experience.
children.contrast: It does not require autobiography, explicit self-concept, language, or reflection.
domains: Components
Often analyzed through perspectivalness, bodily ownership, agency, and pre-reflective self-awareness.

children.label: Embodied / bodily self
children.core: Selfhood organized through the lived body as center of sensation, orientation, action, and vulnerability.
children.contrast: The lived body is not merely the physical body viewed as an external object.
domains: Research
Body ownership and location can be experimentally altered, showing that bodily selfhood is constructed but constrained.

children.label: Perspectival self
children.core: The implicit here–now orientation from which the world is disclosed and possibilities are organized.
children.contrast: It is a structural point of view, not necessarily an explicit representation of ‘me.’
domains: Relation
Closely connected to minimal self and subjectivity.

children.label: Sense of ownership
children.core: The experience that a body part, sensation, thought, or experience is mine.
children.contrast: Ownership differs from agency: a movement can feel mine while not feeling initiated by me.
domains: Example
Passive movement may preserve ownership while reducing agency.

children.label: Self-model
children.core: An internal, embodied, or distributed representation used to predict and regulate the system’s own states, capacities, boundaries, and actions.
children.contrast: A model of self need not be a conscious self or a complete representation of the subject.
domains: AI
System identity, capability estimates, memory summaries, and action-state tracking can form functional self-models.

children.label: Narrative self
children.core: The temporally extended self organized through stories that connect events, motives, roles, values, and anticipated futures.
children.contrast: Narrative selfhood is not the whole of immediate subjectivity and can be revised without erasing every layer of self.
domains: Social
Narratives are co-authored through language, relationships, institutions, and available cultural forms.

children.label: Autobiographical self
children.core: The self organized through personal memories, semantic self-knowledge, continuity, and projected future episodes.
children.contrast: It depends on memory but is not identical to the stored content of memory.
domains: Relation
Overlaps narrative self while emphasizing memory systems and temporal continuity.

children.label: Ego
children.core: A term for self, organizing agency, or the ‘I,’ whose meaning changes radically by tradition.
children.contrast: Never transfer ‘ego’ between ordinary, psychoanalytic, Kantian, and phenomenological contexts without qualification.
domains: Ordinary usage
Self-importance, self-image, or defensive investment in identity.
Psychoanalysis
A regulatory organization mediating drives, reality, defenses, and internalized demands.
Kant
The formal ‘I think’ or unity of apperception, not an experienced inner object.
Husserl
The transcendental or pure ego as pole of intentional acts; its interpretation changes across Husserl’s work.

children.label: Personal identity
children.core: The conditions under which a person at one time is numerically the same person at another time.
children.contrast: It differs from qualitative similarity, personality stability, autobiographical coherence, and legal identification.
domains: Theories
Candidates emphasize bodily continuity, brain continuity, psychological continuity, narrative, or combinations.

children.label: Personhood
children.core: A status associated with being a bearer of reasons, rights, duties, recognition, or morally significant forms of agency and continuity.
children.contrast: Personhood is not synonymous with biological humanity, sentience, intelligence, consciousness, or legal personality; criteria vary by domain.
domains: Ethics
May emphasize rational agency, autonomy, relationships, narrative continuity, or inherent standing.
Law
A legal status assigning rights and liabilities, sometimes to corporations or other nonhuman entities.
AI
No single performance threshold automatically establishes moral or legal personhood.

children.label: Personality
children.core: Relatively stable patterns of affect, motivation, cognition, and behavior across contexts and time.
children.contrast: Personality is not the subject, personal identity, moral character, or total self.
domains: Measurement
Trait models summarize regularities; they do not exhaust situated behavior or lived selfhood.

children.label: Social mind
children.core: Terms concerning how minds perceive, model, affect, coordinate with, and become structured through other minds.
children.contrast: Social cognition is not only private inference about isolated others; interaction and shared practices can partly constitute it.

children.label: Intersubjectivity
children.core: The structure in which multiple subjects encounter, recognize, affect, and correct one another within a shared world.
children.contrast: It is more than agreement and need not reduce other minds to inferred hidden objects.
domains: Phenomenology
Other subjects are encountered as embodied centers of perspective and action; shared objectivity arises within this field.
Social epistemology
Knowledge becomes distributed through testimony, trust, institutions, disagreement, and correction.

children.label: Social cognition
children.core: The capacities used to perceive, interpret, predict, remember, and coordinate with other agents and social situations.
children.contrast: It includes but exceeds explicit theory of mind.
domains: Components
Person perception, emotion recognition, norm learning, attribution, empathy, joint action, and relationship knowledge.

children.label: Theory of mind
children.core: Capacity to attribute perceptions, beliefs, desires, knowledge, intentions, or emotions to oneself and others.
children.contrast: It need not consist of a consciously held scientific-like theory, and it is not equivalent to empathy.
domains: Developmental psychology
Often studied through understanding that another can hold a belief different from reality or one’s own.
AI
Behavioral prediction and explicit state attribution can implement theory-of-mind-like functions without proving experience or moral understanding.

children.label: Mentalizing
children.core: Interpreting behavior in terms of mental states, especially beliefs, desires, feelings, and intentions.
children.contrast: Often used more dynamically and contextually than ‘theory of mind,’ but the terms overlap.
domains: Clinical usage
Includes awareness of uncertainty and the possibility that one’s interpretation of another mind is wrong.

children.label: Empathy
children.core: Responsiveness that apprehends or resonates with another’s perspective or affective state while preserving the self–other distinction.
children.contrast: Empathy is not one faculty and is not identical to sympathy, compassion, agreement, or moral action.

children.label: Cognitive empathy
children.core: Understanding another’s perspective, state, or likely interpretation.
children.contrast: One can understand another accurately without sharing the emotion or caring about the outcome.
domains: Relation
Overlaps perspective-taking and theory of mind.

children.label: Affective empathy
children.core: Affective resonance with another’s emotion while retaining some distinction between their state and one’s own.
children.contrast: Emotional contagion without self–other differentiation is a weaker or different phenomenon.
domains: Risk
High resonance can produce personal distress rather than effective help.

children.label: Compassion
children.core: Concern for another’s suffering joined with motivation to relieve or avoid it.
children.contrast: Compassion does not require reproducing the other’s suffering within oneself.
domains: Contrast
Empathy tracks or resonates; compassion adds benevolent concern and motivation.

children.label: Joint attention
children.core: Two or more subjects attending to the same object while being aware, implicitly or explicitly, of their shared orientation.
children.contrast: It is more than simultaneous attention to one target; the shared relation itself matters.
domains: Role
Supports language learning, teaching, coordination, common ground, and shared relevance.

children.label: Collective intentionality
children.core: Shared forms of intending, believing, accepting, or acting that are structured as ‘we’ rather than as coincident individual states.
children.contrast: Parallel individual goals are not automatically a collective intention.
domains: Examples
Making an agreement, performing together, sustaining an institution, or jointly committing to a plan.

children.label: Communication
children.core: Coordinated production and interpretation of signals that alter another system’s information, expectations, relevance, or action.
children.contrast: Information transfer alone may be too weak for meaning-rich communication; intention and shared conventions vary by case.
domains: Biology
Signals can evolve to influence receivers without reflective communicative intention.
Human language
Meaning depends on syntax, semantics, pragmatics, common ground, embodiment, and social norms.
AI
Generated signals can function communicatively even while questions of intrinsic meaning and intention remain open.

children.label: Language
children.core: A socially shared, generative system of signs and practices for expressing, coordinating, and transforming meaning.
children.contrast: Language is not identical to thought, communication, consciousness, or intelligence, though it restructures each.
domains: Cognitive science
Supports compositional representation, abstraction, instruction, memory, planning, and social learning.
Phenomenology
Provides sedimented public meanings through which self and world become articulable.
AI
Statistical mastery of linguistic practice demonstrates substantial linguistic competence but does not alone settle grounding or experience.

children.label: Normativity
children.core: The dimension of correctness, obligation, permission, reason, and what ought to be done or believed.
children.contrast: Normativity is not reducible to statistical regularity, reward, preference, or social enforcement, though theories differ on its basis.
domains: Mind
Reasons, meanings, promises, beliefs, and responsible agency are partly structured by norms rather than causes alone.
